Buying guide

Buying in Toronto from abroad: what changes

Your citizenship or permanent resident status decides the rules, not where you live. Here is the order I'd work through it, and what to budget.

Ali Bayat
Figures checked against the sources below on November 21, 2026
Published November 26, 2026
4-minute readTime-sensitive rulesUpdated November 2026
The short version
  • Status, not address. Canadian citizens and permanent residents living abroad aren't subject to Ontario's non-resident speculation tax. Foreign nationals generally are.
  • Ontario's tax is 25% of the price for foreign nationals and foreign corporations, with exemptions and rebates that depend on your situation.
  • A federal ban on many purchases by non-Canadians runs to January 1, 2027. Budget 2026 proposes extending it to 2029. Confirm where it stands before you offer.

01The rules that depend on who you are

25%Ontario non-resident speculation taxOn the purchase price, for foreign nationals and foreign corporations buying residential property in Ontario
Jan 1, 2027Federal ban end date in force todayBudget 2026 proposes January 1, 2029 and an exemption for new homes. A proposal, not yet law
WeeksWhat distance adds to the timelineMortgage documents, source of funds and signing from abroad all take time

02From abroad, in order

  1. 01

    Confirm your status first

    Before anything

    Citizen, permanent resident or neither? That decides whether the 25% tax and the federal limits apply, and which exceptions you may qualify for. Your lawyer confirms it.

  2. 02

    Line up money and documents

    Weeks 1–4

    Ask a mortgage broker early. Income earned outside Canada can be treated differently by lenders, and a larger down payment is common. Real estate transactions also require identity verification and a record of where the funds came from.

  3. 03

    Choose a lawyer and how you'll sign

    Weeks 2–4

    Your Ontario real estate lawyer handles title, closing and tax forms. If you can't be here, ask about signing remotely or giving a power of attorney.

  4. 04

    Budget every cost

    Before you offer

    Ontario and Toronto land transfer tax (the calculator shows both), legal fees and, for foreign nationals, the 25% tax unless an exemption applies.

  5. 05

    Plan the money transfer

    Before closing

    International transfers can take days to clear and the amount due at closing is fixed. Start early and keep records of the source.

  6. 06

    Plan for after closing

    Before closing

    Someone has to manage the property: property tax, insurance, maintenance and tenants. Rental income is taxable and non-residents face special withholding rules, so ask an accountant before you buy.

03Watch out for

  • Assuming your address decides itStatus decides, not where you live. A Canadian citizen abroad and a foreign national in Toronto are treated differently.
  • Wire instructions sent by emailConfirm wiring details by phone with your lawyer's office. Fraudulent instructions are a known risk in closings.
  • Buying on photos aloneHave someone you trust, or me, walk the property and the building, and still book the inspection.
Ali's take

From abroad, the risk isn't the price. It's the timeline. Start the paperwork before you start the search.

Quick answers

Do Canadian citizens living abroad pay the non-resident tax?

Ontario says its non-resident speculation tax depends on citizenship or permanent resident status, not on where you live. Ask your lawyer to check your own situation.

Does the 25% tax replace land transfer tax?

No. It is an additional tax. Ontario and, in the City of Toronto, Toronto land transfer tax still apply.

Can I buy a rental property from abroad?

Possibly, depending on your status and the rules in force. Rental income has its own tax treatment for non-residents, so speak to an accountant first.

Buying from outside Canada?

Tell me your status and timeline. I'll lay out the steps and costs for your case, in English or Farsi.
